en: Susiddhikara Ritual for Offerings, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha.
I take refuge in all the Tathāgatas, as well as the Dharma and the assembly of Bodhisattvas.
The Lotus Vajra Family, together with all its retinues—
I now explain the methods of offering and recitation according to the teachings,
omitting repetitions common to the three families, in their proper sequence and correspondence.
First, one should observe the location of the sanctuary, and then clarify its ritual procedures;
next, one receives the true mantra (*mantra*) and learns the method for forming hand gestures (*mudrā*);
finally, regarding the entrances and exits of the exterior area, one performs the method for dividing the ground and purifying it.
Sweep and cleanse the sanctuary, remove withered flowers and the like according to the ritual, and purify the vessels for offerings; thereafter, go to bathe.
First perform the samaya, binding those who would create obstacles.
The methods for expelling obstacles and protecting the body; the rites of luster and water;
bathing and self-consecration; the rite of offering three handfuls of water;
proceeding to the door of the divine chamber; and the rites of changing garments and sprinkling the body.
Upon entering the chamber, one should perform prostrations; then follow the ritual for preparing the various offerings:
the rosary, the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), the *kuśa* grass ring, and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
One should present the *argha* water and perform the ritual for arranging the seat.
Furthermore, one observes the samaya: the dharmas for removing bodily obstacles and hindrances;
the dharmas for expelling and cleansing defilements to achieve purity and luster;
and the dharmas for protecting the body, establishing the boundary, and [guarding] the eight directions, above, and below.
First, one should visualize the divine seat and contemplate the dharma of the tutelary deity;
according to the specific location, one should invoke the dharma of the tutelary deity;
having invoked the tutelary deity with their respective root mantras, [one proceeds].
Immediately dispel [obstacles] from Māra, and offer a seat for the deity to sit;
then observe the samaya, immediately offer argha water, and perform the rite of bathing the Honored One and offering robes.
Next, offer unguents, flowers, incense, food, and drink; perform the rite of offering lamps;
employ the mantras and mudrās, as well as the mental visualization for making offerings;
perform the praises, repentances, and so forth; and protect both the honored deity and yourself.
And protect that location by performing the rite for binding the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*);
prepare the vajra and the methods for the rosary and so forth;
fulfill the section on mantras, followed by the method for sitting and reciting.
Request the fulfillment of one's original vows, protect the recitation being performed,
dedicate the merit of the Dharma, and give rise to vast aspirations;
furthermore, offer argha water, anoint with unguents, burn incense, and perform other such rites.
Furthermore, one should observe the samaya, protect the body and oneself,
and release the boundaries previously established; thereafter, perform the dismissal of the deities,
as well as the homa and its constituent parts, including the hearth-deity and the earth.
The ritual for performing fire offerings;
the method for reciting Vaipulya sutras and constructing caityas;
followed by the practice of meditative contemplations such as loving-kindness, and the method for reflecting upon the six recollections.
Such sequences as these have now been briefly explained by me.
As for "one who sees the location of the divine chamber," this refers to one who enters the maṇḍala, upon which flower falls, and takes refuge in that deity.

Regarding the clarification of the ritual methods: this refers to having received the supreme initiation of the vidyā-mantra, being authorized by the ācārya, and being permitted to transmit the dharma-initiation, as well as to perform other various initiations such as those for pacifying calamities (*śāntika*).

Regarding those who receive mantras and mudrās: the recipient, having bathed for purification and donned fresh, clean garments, shall kneel in the *pralambapādāsana* posture at a pure location and, with reverence toward the ācārya, personally receive the mantra and perform the mudrā.
At that time, the ācārya first recites it three times and transmits it to the other.
Having received it, the latter recites it himself three times; giving rise to profound joy, he receives and upholds it with the highest reverence—this constitutes the mutual reception.
Having made offerings to the ācārya according to one’s capacity and having extensively understood the Dharma, one may then proceed with this sequence of recitation.

Regarding the external places of entry and exit: once one has risen in the early morning, wherever one goes—even to impure places—one must protect the body by using the *āveśana-mantra* (the mantra of wrathful penetration).

The mantra is: Oṃ kuru tvaṃ hūṃ jaḥ. As for the mudrā: form a fist with the right hand, extend the thumb straight upward, and place it upon five locations—namely, the crown of the head, the two shoulders, the heart, and above the throat.

Regarding the division of earth for cleansing: one should use five portions of earth to wash the lower part; three portions to wash the urinary area; three portions to touch and wash the left hand; and seven portions to wash both hands together. If one fears it is not yet clean, one may wash as much as desired, with cleanliness as the limit.

Third, regarding the three heaps of earth: seal the earth with the *sparśana-mantra* and the hand gesture (*mudrā*), recite the mantra seven times over each heap, and then use them; next, use the mantra to sprinkle water upon one's own body.
The mantra is: *Rāṇi Hūṃ Ha*.

Recite this three times. As for the mudrā: with the right hand, palm facing upward, extend the five fingers straight with their tips touching. Next, bend the middle joint of the ring finger so that it aligns with the palm. Then, bend the thumb and place it against the base of the index finger, pointing forward.
As for the method of sprinkling water: face east, squat silently, place both hands between the knees, cup the water with the hand-mudrā, and drink it without bubbles and without making a sound.
Having drunk three times, one then uses the hand to moisten water and wipes the lips twice.

At that time, as impurities may touch the tongue between the teeth within the mouth, or during sneezing or coughing, one again drinks water and wipes the lips as before. Then, using this same mudrā and reciting the mantra, one first touches the two eyes, followed by the mouth, the two ears, the nose, the two shoulders, the throat, the navel, the heart, the throat [again], and the crown of the head; thus the body is protected and the sense faculties are purified.

"Sweeping and cleaning the divine chamber" means that, in accordance with one's accomplishments and the specific requirements of the rite, one selects a location that is appropriate for those [deities] and pleasing to the mind, free from all obstacles and difficulties.

The site should be cleared of *vālmīka* (anthills), insect nests, pits, hollows, rubble, chaff, bones, hair, ash, charcoal, and salt; having excavated the impure soil and filled it with pure earth, one should construct a chamber upon it, making it firm and airtight so that no wind may enter. The door should open toward the east, or north, or west, or toward the south according to the specific purpose of the rite.

Once the divine chamber has been constructed, smear it with cow dung and sprinkle it with pure water; or, using fragrant ointment mixed with pure water, one should apply it to the ground while reciting this vidyā-mantra.
The mantra says: *Namaḥ saptānīyakānanasattvārthata*.
Gatramire vire maheśvara vajri sarvata sarvata sara sara tatraiḥ.

*Tara yi vīta maṃ niṃ saṃ bañña niṃ ta ra maṃ ti siddha gṛhe tvaṃ svāhā.* If at times one forgets the recitation or the ritual procedure is erroneous, thereby violating the *samaya*, [one should perform this].
Every day one should recite this vidyā three, seven, or one hundred and eight times; it can eliminate those faults.
Regarding the removal of withered flowers: after having made offerings of noble flowers, one should first recite this vidyā to remove the withered ones.
He said:
"Oṃ śviti ti ma ha śviti kha na naṃ svāhā. Next, he spoke the mantra for sweeping the ground.
The mantra is: Oṃ hrala hrala ruru ghara hrala naya svāhā. Next, the mantra for smearing the ground is recited.

The *Vidyā* says: "Recite three times: Oṃ kare kare mahe kare svāhā. First, one should sprinkle and sweep the shrine room, remove withered flowers, and purify all the offering vessels; only then should one go to bathe. Such is the instruction.
When going to bathe, first protect all the offering implements with this mantra and mudrā, and only then may you proceed. The mantra is:
*Oṃ śukra vajri āḥ*.

Recite this three times. As for the form of the mudrā: make a fist with the right hand, extend the thumb straight up, and touch all the offering implements while joining the index and middle fingers together to empower them.

Regarding "first performing the samaya": this means that whenever one performs a ritual, one must first perform the samaya, and only thereafter perform all other matters such as the protection of the body; thus it is taught.
Next, the samaya mantras and mudrās are explained.

First, the mantra of the Buddha Family is: *Oṃ tathāgataduhitṛ-nābha-vāya svāhā*. Recite this three times. As for the form of its mudrā: extend the ten fingers of both hands upward, straight forward, with the palms side by side and touching; slightly bend the upper joints of the two index fingers. This is the samaya-mudrā of the Buddha Family.
Next, the *samaya* mantra and mudrā of the Padma family are explained.

The mantra is: "Oṃ namo nāthavayā svāhā. Recite this three times. As for the characteristics of the mudrā: first, join the palms; extend the two middle sets of six fingers outward so that they do not touch one another; keep the thumbs and little fingers of both hands joined as usual. Within the hollowed palms, let them be like a lotus flower spread out, with the six extended fingers slightly bent. This is the *samaya* mudrā of the Padma family.
Next, the samaya mantra and mudrā of the Vajra Family are explained.

The mantra is: Oṃ vajranātha svāhā. Recite this three times. As for the form of the mudrā: place the right hand over the left, with the backs of both hands joined together. Insert the right thumb through the space between the fingers of the left little finger, and insert the left thumb through the space between the fingers of the right little finger. Slightly separate the six middle fingers of both hands so that they resemble a three-pronged vajra; this is the Vajrasamaya Mudrā.
Next, regarding the binding of all obstacles: this refers to binding all obstacles by means of the *Muṇḍarī* hand-seal (*mudrā*) and mantra.

As for the characteristics of the seal: place the left hand upon the right shoulder; with the thumb, pinch the nail of the little finger, and extend the middle three fingers like a three-pronged vajra.
Again, place the right hand upon the left shoulder, pressing the thumb against the nail of the little finger, and extend the middle three fingers like a three-pronged pestle.

Standing facing east, bend the knee of the left leg and bring it forward toward the body; extend the right leg wide for about two chi and plant it flat on the ground. Bite the lower lip near its edge, glare with angry eyes looking to the left, and silently visualize yourself as Kuntali.
Recite this root mantra: *Namaḥ ratnatrayāya namaḥ*.

Those various obstacles will then become fetters.
Next, regarding the method for bathing: in order to purify the body, first take pure earth and divide it into three portions, reciting the mantra and performing the mudrā over each one.
The mantra is as follows, accompanied by the Three Profound and Wondrous Seals:

"Oṃ niḥ khaṃ vaṃ sute svāhā. Recite this five times; this is the mantra of the Pure Land. As for the mudrā: interlace the two hands with the fingers tucked behind the backs of the hands. Extend both index fingers upright and touch them together. Place both thumbs side-by-side, upright, alongside the sides of the index fingers.
Touch the earth to be taken with this mudrā, recite the mantra five times, and then take it.
Next, regarding the expulsion [of obstructors]: for all activities one undertakes, one must first perform the expulsion before proceeding with any task; such is the instruction taught.
The mantra for expelling obstructors is: *Namaḥ vajrāya hūṃ haṃ namaḥ ṭuṃ namaḥ maṃ svasti vidyābhyo rakṣa*.
Recite "YAṂ HŪṂ VAṂ PHAṬ" seven times; this is the mantra for expelling obstructors. As for the mudrā:

with the left hand, bend the thumb into the palm, press the thumb with the middle and ring fingers, bend the index finger so that its tip rests against the side of the middle joint of the middle finger, and likewise bend the little finger.
Pointing to the side of the middle joint of the ring finger, extend and straighten the arm; rotate it three times clockwise above the head and seal the five places of the body.
Press the thumb of the right hand against the nail of the little finger, with the remaining three fingers held upright to form the shape of a *vajra*;
cross them at the side of the waist and establish the posture as before—this is the rite for warding off [evil].
The mudrā for expulsion.
Furthermore, the mantra and hand-mudrā for warding off [obstacles].
The mantra is as follows:
"Oṃ vajratraḥ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra for expulsion. As for the mudrā: strike the palm of the right hand against the palm of the left hand three times; this is the mudrā for expulsion.
Furthermore, there are the mantra and mudrā for expelling obstructors.

The mantra is: "Oṃ kīlikīlilaya vajra ḍhaṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra for expelling obstructors. As for the form of the mudrā: snap the fingers with the right hand three times; this is the mudrā for expelling obstructors.
Next, regarding the method for protecting the body: one should use this mantra and mudrā to bind the boundaries of the ten directions and to protect the body.

The mantra is: Oṃ śaṃkara-samaya-hūṃ svāhā. This is the mantra for binding the boundaries and protecting the body. As for the form of the mudrā: with the right hand, press the thumb against the nail of the little finger, while the remaining three fingers are slightly spread and held upright; this is called the Vajra-mudrā. It is used to bind the boundaries above, below, and in the eight directions, as well as to protect the body.
Next, one should seal one's own body with mantras and mudrās; by means of water, earth, soap powder, and other such substances, impurities are thereby removed and purification is accomplished.

The mantra is: “Oṃ kili kili vajra hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this seven times; it is the mantra for removing impurities. As for the mudrā: with the right hand, press the thumb upon the nail of the little finger, while the remaining three fingers are slightly spread and held upright, crossed at the waist with the three fingers pointing forward. Perform this same mudrā with the left hand as well. By touching various objects with these hands, they are immediately cleansed and purified. This is the mudrā for removing impurities.
Next, perform purification using the mantra and mudrā of Kuṇḍalī.

The mantra is: *Oṃ amṛte hūṃ phaṭ*. As for the form of the mudrā: form a fist with the right hand to take water; recite the mantra seven times and sprinkle it upon all objects and one’s own head, whereby they become purified. This is the purification mudrā; in this fist, the four fingers should not touch the palm.
Next, use the mantra and mudrā to produce radiance. The mantra is: *Oṃ jvala jvalaya vana li svāhā*.

Recite this three times; this is the mantra for radiance. As for the form of the mudrā: with the left hand, press the thumb upon the nail of the little finger, keep the remaining three fingers slightly spread and held upright, and extend the elbow. Then, with the right hand, form this same seal to support the underside of the left elbow. By touching various objects or one's own body with the left-hand seal, radiance is produced; this is the mudrā of radiance.
Next, stir the water with a mantra and mudrā. The mantra is: *Oṃ hūṃ ha na va jri va jri ṇa ha*.

This is the mantra for stirring the water. As for the characteristics of the mudrā: interlace the two hands outwardly, bend them against the backs of the hands, place both thumbs bent within the palms, and slightly bend the tips of the two index fingers so that their nails touch one another; this is the water-stirring mudrā.
Next, take earth with mantra and mudrā to smear upon the body.

The mantra is: *Oṃ bhūrja vaḥ hūṃ*. Recite this seven times; this is the mantra for smearing the body. As for the form of the mudrā: take earth mixed with water, place the thumbs of both hands respectively upon the nails of the little fingers, extend the remaining fingers, and rub them against one another. Then, using the right hand, smear it all over the body; this is the mudrā for washing the body with earth.
Next, using the mantra and mudrā of Kuṇḍalī, recite the water-mantra as follows:

"Oṃ āṃ mṛte hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this seven times. As for the form of the mudrā: first extend the right hand flat; first bend the middle finger and ring finger to press upon the nails of the thumbs; slightly bend the index and little fingers toward the sides of the middle and ring fingers. While reciting the mantra, stir the water with the mudrā; perform the ritual bathing while reciting the water-mudrā.
Next, one should dispel the Vighnas within the body by means of mantras and mudrās.

The mantra is: *Oṃ āṃ mṛte hana hana hūṃ phaṭ; remove the Vighnas from within the body.* As for the form of the mudrā: with both hands, bend the thumbs into the palms and clench each hand into a fist. Extend the two index fingers and interlace them left and right into the "tiger's mouth. Move this seal from the crown of the head down to the feet and then release it. This is the mudrā for dispelling the Vighnas within the body.
Next, one should protect the five parts of the body with the mantra and mudrā of Kuntali. The mantra is: Oṃ vajra-jñiṇi-pratini-pata-ya svāhā (the mantra for protecting the body).

As for the form of the mudrā: interlace the two little fingers and insert them into the palms; press the two ring fingers down upon the two upright little fingers; touch the tips of the two middle fingers together on their sides; slightly bend the two index fingers so that they stand upright on the side of the first phalanges of the middle fingers, separated by the distance of a single grain of barley; place the two thumbs on the side of the middle fingers. By touching the five parts of the body with this seal, protection is accomplished; this is the protection seal.
Next, using the mantra and mudrā, recite over each portion of the earth separately.

The mantra is: *Oṃ dhu dhu ka ya dhu bhi pra īva ri ṇi svāhā*. Recite this mantra three times. As for the form of the mudrā: join the tips of the two index fingers and the two little fingers; bend the two middle fingers and the two ring fingers into the palms; keep the backs of the two hands together so they do not touch; and join the sides of the tips of the two thumbs. Take one portion from the three heaps of earth previously set out, seal the earth with this mudrā, and recite the mantra three times while using it to wash from the feet to the navel; then wash one's hands and sprinkle water for purification.
The second and third times are likewise washed and purified with sprinkling.
Again, take one portion and, reciting as before, use it to wash from the navel to the neck;
again, take one portion and, reciting as before, use it to wash from the neck to the crown of the head.
Having finished, one should again recite the mantra and perform the hand-seal (*mudrā*).

At will, having washed oneself, one should again perform this seal and likewise recite the mantra; while maintaining the hand-seal, rotate it all over the body, releasing the seal at the heart and behind the back. This is called the Armor Seal (*kavaca-mudrā*).
This is the earth-purifying mudrā.
Next, recite the root mantra of Kuntali and stir the water with your hand, bathing as you wish.
The mantra is as follows:
Namo ratnatrayāya | Namaḥ śrīvajrapāṇaye | Namah | Namo.

As for the self-consecration, perform the self-consecration with this mantra and mudrā.

The mantra is: Oṃ hakharihari hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this three times; it is the initiation mantra (*abhiṣeka-mantra*). As for the mudrā: interlace the two little fingers and insert them into the palms. Place the two ring fingers side by side, pressing down upon the crossed little fingers, and hold them upright. Bring the tips of the two middle fingers together so they touch. Position the two index fingers beside the [other] index fingers. Using this mudrā, take water and recite the mantra three times while performing self-initiation; this is the initiation mudrā.
Next, one should bind one’s hair using the mantra and mudrā. The mantra is: *Oṃ susiddhi-kari svāhā*. Recite this three times;

it is used for all three families (*trikula*). As for the form of the mudrā: form a fist with the right hand, extend the thumb straight, and press the tip of the index finger against the tip of the thumb so that they are bound together in a circular curve. Having performed this mudrā and recited the mantra three times, place it upon the crown of the head; this constitutes the Hair-Binding Mudrā (*keśabandhana-mudrā*).
The mantra for binding the hair of the Buddha Family is:
"Oṃ śi-ki-śi-khe svāhā. Recite this three times. The mantra for binding the hair of the Lotus Family is:
"Oṃ śi-khe svāhā. Recite this three times. The mantra for binding the hair of the Vajra Family is:

"Oṃ śikṣā svāhā. (Recite three times. Whenever one bathes, one should not do so in muddy water, nor in water containing thorns, nor in water from steep banks, nor in shallow water from narrow channels, nor in swirling or turbulent currents, nor in turbid water teeming with insects, nor in irrigation water for fields, nor in water from pits... one must not bathe in such waters as these.
Furthermore, one should not defecate or urinate in the water or on its banks; nor should one engage in such games as leaping, running, rushing about, floating, or submerging oneself within the water.

While in the water, do not look at private parts; nor should you dwell upon the private parts of women, nor their breasts, waists, or any other limbs. You should bathe in silence and stillness, merely to remove impurities, without the thought of adorning the body.

Next, regarding the offering of three handfuls of water: having finished the ritual bathing, face the direction where the deity resides and visualize the deity. Recite the mantra and perform the mudrā; with the hand forming the mudrā, scoop up water and offer three handfuls. Visualize bathing the deity and presenting *argha* (offering water), or [visualize it] within the water itself. Recite the mantra according to your intention, and only then proceed to the maṇḍala site.
The mantra for offering water to the Buddha Family is: *Oṃ tīraḥ pūjita svāhā*. Recite this three times and offer three handfuls of water.
The mantra for offering water to the Lotus Family is: *Oṃ bari bari hūṃ phaṭ*. Recite this three times and offer three handfuls of water. The mantra for offering water to the Vajra Family is:

"Oṃ viśvavajra svāhā. Recite this three times while offering water with cupped hands. As for the mudrā: place both hands palms up, side by side, and touching; join the tips of the two index fingers with the tips of the two thumbs; slightly bend the remaining six fingers. Using this mudrā to cup water, recite the mantra and offer it three times to bathe the Honored One (Bhagavat). This mudrā for offering the three cups of water is common to all three families.
Once the offerings have been completed and the ritual ablutions finished, the various mudrās employed during the interrogation must be released.
By means of the *asamajñāna* mantra, turning the hand-mudrā counter-clockwise constitutes the untying of the knots.

The mantra is: Oṃ āḥ samayajñānī kṛiṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra for dissolving the boundary (*sīmā*). As for the mudrā: place the back of the right hand within the left palm so that there is no gap between them; extend both thumbs upward and straight. Rotate [the hands] once to the left to dissolve the previously bound seal. Regarding those who proceed to the *maṇḍala*: when entering toward the *maṇḍala*, one must not give rise to anger or greed, but should proceed while focusing single-mindedly on the *iṣṭadevatā*.

Within the sanctuary, one must not step over various weapons or medicinal herbs—namely, diverse vessels, mounts, bells, ritual implements, withered flowers, medicinal essences, and all plants and trees; nor should one step over the shadows of caityas, honored images, or bhikṣus. Furthermore, one must not ride elephants, horses, camels, oxen, sheep, donkeys, or any other vehicles, nor should one touch them with the hands or body.
If one commits these [transgressions], one falls from the *samaya* and must likewise not give rise to greed, hatred, delusion, pride, agitation, arrogance, and so forth.

One should go to the *maṇḍala* wearing wooden sandals; however, upon encountering a *caitya*, a venerable image, or one’s preceptor and teachers, one should remove the wooden sandals, pay due respect, and only then enter the *maṇḍala*.

Regarding "sprinkling the body and changing clothes": this means that upon arriving outside the gate of the ritual arena (maṇḍala), one stands there, washes the hands and feet, and again drinks water and performs the purification by sprinkling using the previously mentioned mantras and mudrās.
The mantra for drinking water and sprinkling for purification in the Buddha Family is:
"Oṃ maho-jvala hūṃ. The mantra for drinking water and sprinkling for purification in the Lotus Family is:
"Oṃ dhu dhu ra kru ru kru ru svāhā. The mantra for drinking water and sprinkling for purification in the Vajra Family is:

"Oṃ jvalitavajriṇi hūṃ. This is the mudrā for drinking water and sprinkling for purification belonging to the Buddha Family. Extend the right hand upward, bend the middle joint of the ring finger inward, and do not let it touch the palm.

Next, the mudrā for drinking water and sprinkling for purification in the Lotus Family is explained: extend the right hand upward, bend the middle joints of the ring finger and the little finger inward, and ensure they do not touch the palm.

Regarding the mudrā for drinking water and sprinkling for purification in the Vajra Family: extend the right hand upward, bend the ring finger inward so that it does not touch the palm, and spread the index and little fingers apart.
Next, purify the robes that have been changed outside the gate using mantras and mudrās.

The mantra is: "Oṃ Vimala Svāhā. This is the mantra for sprinkling the robes. As for the form of the mudrā: form a fist with the right hand, take water, and while reciting the mantra, sprinkle it upon the purified robes.
Next, one should don the robe after consecrating it with the mantra.

The mantra is: *Oṃ parivāradavajri hūṃ*. Regarding "entering the room and performing prostrations," as stated in the instructions, the practitioner should enter the maṇḍala with a single-minded focus.

You have descended here by the power of your original vows; we pray that you will bestow your empowerment, accept this invitation, and receive these various offerings prepared by us. Arising in great compassion, please deign to accept them."
Having taken [the offerings], one should place them below the principal deity, the *vināyakas* who follow and pursue him, and the *samaya*.
If garments, necklaces, and other such items have been prepared, one should offer them while reciting the *karmasādhana-mantra*.

Regarding the method for establishing the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*): one establishes the boundary of the ground using the *vajra-kīla* rite, and establishes the boundary of the upper direction using the *vajra-prākāra*.
The mantra of the *vajra-kīla* is: "Oṃ kili kili vajra phaṭ."
Recite "Līṃ Vūṃ Phaṭ" three times. As for the mudrā:
extend the middle and ring fingers of the left hand outward, insert them between the middle and ring fingers of the right hand, and twist the left ring finger.

Insert the back of the right ring finger into the palm of the right hand; twist the middle finger of the left hand around the back of the right middle finger and insert it into the palm of the right hand.
Join the two little fingers and the two index fingers together. Extend the two thumbs straight upward with their tips touching.
Form this mudrā by spreading the two arms like wings, causing the two thumbs to... [be joined].
Touching the fingertips to the ground, recite the mantra to establish the boundary of the earth using the Vajra Stake mudrā.
Next, use the Vajra Fence mantra and its corresponding mudrā to establish the boundary of the upper direction.

The mantra is: Oṃ veśapraṇarākṣa vajra-phaṭ ja ra hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this three times. As for the mudrā: following the previous *kīla* (stake) mudrā, change only by placing the two thumbs side-by-side against the sides of the two index fingers. Holding the mudrā upward while reciting the mantra accomplishes the binding of the empty realm; this is the Vajra Hook Fence Mudrā.
The mantra and mudrā of the Vajra Wall. The mantra of the Vajra Wall is:

*Oṃ sara sara vajraprakāra hūṃ phaṭ*. As for the form of its mudrā: based on the previous *kīlana* (nailing) mudrā, simply change the two thumbs so they are spread apart and held upright. Perform this mudrā three times, rotating from the south to the right while reciting the mantra; this accomplishes the Vajra Wall mudrā, which is also the Vajra Furnace mudrā.
Next, bind the boundary of the eastern direction with the Vajrapāśa mantra and mudrā.

The mantra is: "Oṃ vajrapāśa hṛdaya ga ga na ma ra hūṃ. Recite this three times. As for the form of the mudrā: bend the left index finger beneath the base of the thumb; extend the left thumb straight upward, pressing against the nail of the index finger, leaving a small circular opening. Extend the remaining three fingers straight up, touching them together. The right hand is likewise positioned, with the backs of the three right fingers placed against the inner side of the three left fingers. This is the Vajrapāśa mudrā.
Next, one should bind the boundary of the western direction with the Vajradhvaja mantra and mudrā.

The mantra is: "Oṃ padma kīli kīlaya hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this three times. As for the form of the mudrā: make a fist with the left hand and extend the thumb straight up; extend the five fingers of the right hand and place them sideways upon the tip of the left thumb, with the palm facing the body. This is the Vajradhvaja-fist mudrā for binding the western boundary.
The right hand is positioned as the left; this is also that same mudrā.
Next, one binds the northern boundary with the mantra and mudrā of Vajrakālī.
The mantra is as follows:

"Oṃ vajragarjita maṭha. Recite this three times. As for the mudrā: join the tips of the thumbs and little fingers of both hands together; bend the remaining fingers individually toward the palms so that the backs of the fingers do not touch one another nor the palms. This binds the northern boundary and is the Vajragarjita mudrā.
Next, one should bind the southern boundary with the Vajraśikhara mantra and mudrā.

The mantra is: “Oṃ vajraśikhara ruṭ maṭ. Recite this three times. As for the form of the hand-mudrā: form a fist with the left hand and extend the thumb straight up; do the same with the right hand, placing it upon the tip of the left thumb, so that the tips of the right thumb and index finger press together.

Furthermore, based on this mudrā, one binds the boundary of the South; however, one merely changes it by extending straight the three fingers below the right middle finger. This is also called the *śṛṅga-mudrā* (Peak Mudrā), which binds the boundary of the South; it is the Vajra-Śṛṅga Mudrā.

Next, recite the mantra seven times over the palm of the right hand and point it toward the ground to establish the boundary of the lower direction; then, with the same mudrā, turn the hand upward and strike the space above to likewise establish the boundary of the upper direction.
The mantra is: "Oṃ śaṅkare svāhā. Recite this seven times. Next, using the asaṃgajina mantra and its mudrā, universally construct the fire enclosure.
The mantra is as follows:

As for the mudrā, place the back of the right hand within the left hand so that there are no gaps between them; extend both thumbs upward and straight. Turning once to the right completes the fire enclosure; this is the *asamañjiṇī* mudrā.
Next, one should re-establish the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) by means of mantras and mudrās. The mantra is: "Oṃ śaṅkara-maṅgala-saṃyama svāhā. Recite this seven times;

it is the mantra for binding the Great Boundary within the threefold boundary. As for the form of the mudrā: interlace the little fingers and ring fingers of both hands, placing them inside the palms. Straighten the two middle fingers so that their tips touch. Bend the two index fingers over the second phalanges on the backs of the middle fingers, ensuring they do not touch the middle fingers, resembling a three-pronged vajra. Place the two thumbs beside the index fingers and rotate [the hands] toward the eight directions, above, and below while reciting the mantra. This completes the binding of the Great Boundary; this is the Great Boundary-binding mudrā.

Having performed this, even if those near the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin or other opposing mantra-practitioners should attempt to cause destruction, they will be unable to do so, nor can they diminish the majesty and power of the deity; furthermore, all methods for breaking vidyā-mantras, binding them, or reversing their effects shall find no opportunity to prevail.

Next, regarding "preparing the vajra and so forth," this refers to items such as a vajra, a rosary, a ring, a waist-cord, armlets, a lotus, and a banner. These should be purified with scented water or other substances and consecrated by reciting the mantra of the deity. One must possess the aforementioned items during both the time of recitation (*japa*) and the time of fire ritual (*homa*).

Next, the methods for accomplishing various other objects, such as the vajra and so forth, shall be explained. Regarding the vajra, it should be placed within a vessel according to its corresponding requirements and positioned upon a seat directly in front of oneself; it should then be anointed with white sandalwood, saffron, and red sandalwood incense, each used according to its respective category.

Next, holding incense, flowers, and so forth, one should perform offerings and invite the lords of mantras, such as Vajrapāṇi. By reciting their respective mantras while offering the incense and flowers, and further reciting them one thousand times, it is called "accomplishment" (siddhi).
The mantra for this Vajra is: Oṃ dhuvaṃ vajrahā. This accomplishes the Vajra-mantra.
One should fashion a three-pronged *vajra* from red sandalwood and other materials and perform one thousand recitations.

Next, the mantra for purifying the rosary of the Buddha Family (*buddhakula*) is stated as follows: *Namo ratnatrayāya | oṃ ānate vi-jaye siddhisiddhe svāhā* Next, the mantra for purifying the rosary of the Lotus Family (*padmakula*) is stated as follows:
*Namo vighnāntakṛt vajrāya oṃ aṃ mṛtyuñjaya śrīye śrīmaṃ niri svāhā*. Next, the mantra for purifying the rosary of the Vajra family is spoken:

"Namo ratnatrayāya | namaḥ śrīvajrapāṇaye | mahākṣasūtrāya | oṃ kili kili lalini svāhā. With these three-part mantras for purifying the rosary beads, one should thread the beads according to the specific mantra of their respective family, reciting each individual bead seven times until the threading is complete.
Furthermore, recite the mantra one hundred times and purify the rosary again according to the previous method; thereafter, perform the accomplishment (*sādhana*) using this mantra.
First, the mantra for accomplishing the rosary of the Buddha Family (*buddhakula*) is stated as follows:
Oṃ namo bhagavate siddhe śāstāya siddhārthi svāhā. Next, the mantra for accomplishing the rosary of the Lotus Family (*padmakula*) is stated as follows:
Oṃ va-su-ma-nti śrī-ye pa-taṃ maṃ-gali-ni svā-hā. The mantra for the rosary of accomplishment for the Vajra Family is: Oṃ vajra-īḍan-jaye svā-hā.

With this mantra for the rosary of accomplishment, one should invoke the mantra of the specific family upon the rosary, and perform the recitation a thousand times as an offering to achieve accomplishment.

Next, the characteristics of the mudrā for holding the rosary are explained: with the right hand, press the tip of the ring finger with the thumb; extend the middle and little fingers straight; slightly bend the tip of the index finger and place it against the side of the upper joint of the middle finger. This mudrā is used for all three families; it is the rosary mudrā of the Buddha Family.

Next, the mudrā for holding the rosary in the Lotus Family is described: with the right hand, press the tip of the middle finger with the thumb, and extend the remaining three fingers straight; the left hand is likewise positioned.
Next, the mudrā for holding a rosary in the Vajra Family is described: form a fist with the right hand, extend the thumb, and press the index finger; do the same with the left hand.
One should use *akṣa* seeds for the Buddha family as a rosary, *padmākṣa* seeds for the Avalokiteśvara family as a rosary, and *rudrākṣa* seeds for the Vajra family as a rosary.

Furthermore, it is said: take either *jīvaputra*, *padmabīja*, *rudrākṣa*, conch shell, or stones from the *śrīphala* tree; or gold, silver, iron, lead, tin, refined copper, lapis lazuli, or any one of these, numbering more than a hundred, and fashion them into a rosary. Holding it in the right hand with an undistracted mind, once the recitation of the mantra is complete, one should count the beads all at once, ensuring that no counting occurs before or after [the recitation].

Next, the method for the armlet is explained: within the armlet, one should thread a bead made from the heartwood of a living tree. Using the mantra and mudrā of the Family Mother (*kulamātṛ*), one should recite it while making offerings of incense and flowers, sprinkling with scented water, and invoking her with the same Family Mother mantra and mudrā to empower the armlet. Furthermore, one should perform the offerings in sequence with the Family Mother mantra and mudrā until the mantra has been recited one thousand times.

Fashion a ring from *nāba* grass and place it on the ring finger; using the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*) of the respective family, perform the ritual as previously described for accomplishment, reciting it up to one thousand times, following the sequence of each respective family as should be understood.

Regarding the method for the waist-band: have a young girl twist and join the thread, dyeing it with *kusumbha*—here translated as red-blue flower—or saffron. Having accomplished the practice through the aforementioned ritual up to one thousand recitations, wear it around the waist during recitation, during *homa*, and while sleeping; this will prevent the loss of semen.
The mantra for accomplishing the waist-line is:
"Oṃ hara hara bama dama niṣkrama draṇi siddhaḥ svāhā. It is used for all three families; its mudrā is the same as that of the Family Mother (Kulamātṛ).
Within the Buddha Family, the thread is white; within the Lotus Family, the thread is yellow; and within the Vajra Family, the thread is red.
Only when these materials are fully prepared upon one's person may the ritual be performed, according to the sūtras and the respective families, as explained in the scriptures.

Once the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) has been established, one should next perform the offerings. According to the specific accomplishment and the particular class of the ritual manual (*kriyā-tantra*), one should prepare unguents whose color, taste, and fragrance correspond to those [deities]. These should possess the qualities previously described, from the removal of impurities up to the attainment of luster.
The unguent should be consecrated by reciting this mantra and the mantra of the specific family (*kula*), and then offered while forming the hand gesture (*mudrā*).
The mantra for offering the unguent is as follows: *I me yan da śu bha ni vi ya śu*.
Jña ya śu jña ya yu na ya maṃ nya ni ve ni du ba kṣi-tya pra-ti gṛ-hya pra-si no.
Recite "Oṃ ahara ahara sarvavighnān daha svāhā" seven times; this may be used for all three families. As for the mudrā: extend the right hand.
With the five fingers extended and the palms facing outward, use the left hand to grasp the wrist of the right hand from above;
extend the four fingers outward and hold them with the thumb inside. This is the mudrā for offering scented unguents (gandha), used for all three families.

Furthermore, the mantra for offering scented unguent (*vilepana*) to the Buddha Family is: "Oṃ akṣaratāragraveśanamaḥ svāhā. Recite this seven times. The mantra for offering scented unguent to the Lotus Family is:
"Oṃ jñānajñānajñaṭapane jñātaye jñaptaye panine hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this seven times. The mantra for offering scented unguent to the Vajra Family is:

"Oṃ vīrasara vīrasara hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this seven times. Next, regarding the removal of impurities and the attainment of luster as previously described, one should consecrate the flowers with this mantra as well as the root mantra, and then offer them while performing the hand gesture (mudrā).
The Mantra for Offering Flowers is as follows: "I me su maṅgala su ni viya śu jña śu jña yu maṅga ya maṅgala ya."
Nirvṛta-prakṣaya-prahīṇa-prasāda oṃ aha-ra aha-ra sarva-rava-vi.
*Niyadra-pūjite svāhā*. Recite this seven times; it is the mantra for offering flowers, applicable to all three families.

The hand gesture (*mudrā*) is the same as the previous chariot seal (*ratha-mudrā*), with the exception that the two thumbs are spread across the sides of the two index fingers. This is the flower-offering seal, used for all three families.
Furthermore, the mantra for offering flowers to the Buddha Family is:
"Oṃ śi ki śi ke svāhā. Recite this seven times. The mantra for offering flowers to the Lotus Family is:
"Oṃ jani-kanthamud-dhini hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this seven times. The mantra for offering flowers to the Vajra Family is:

"Oṃ pūrjvalanta-pratye svāhā. Recite this seven times. Next, for the removal of impurities and up to the application of luster as previously described, one should burn incense while reciting these mantras and the root mantras, and further offer it by forming the mudrās.
The mantra for offering incense is: *Ā Vajranati-sugandha-jāty-agarū*.
*Sura-bhojanaṃ maṃjuśrīye bhaktyā nivedayāmi | pratigṛhṇātu oṃ* (3 syllables) *durbodhyam-vara-pratigṛhṇāhi yan*. Oṃ. (3 syllables).
Recite "A-ha-ra a-ha-ra sa-ra-ba vi-ni-ya da-ra-pu-rī-te svā-hā" seven times; this may be used for all three families.
As for the mudrā: with the little fingers and [ring fingers] of both hands...
The ring fingers and middle fingers are placed together with their backs facing inward and extended straight upward;
the two index fingers are held side by side, separated by the distance of one grain of barley without touching; and the two thumbs are pressed against the sides of the two index fingers.
This is the seal for offering incense, common to all three families.
The mantra for offering incense to the Buddha Family is:
“Namaḥ krodhamanavīśaye śrīṇi svāhā. Recite seven times. The mantra for offering incense to the Lotus Family is:
“Oṃ jvalara-bhavana gariṇa giriṇi hūṃ phaṭ. Recite seven times. The mantra for offering incense to the Vajra Family is:

"Oṃ veśvara veśvara hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this seven times. Next, for the removal of impurities as previously described, up to the application of luster, one should consecrate the food and drink with this mantra and the root mantra, and then offer it while forming the hand gestures (mudrās).
The mantra for offering food is:
*Oṃ āh hīḥ sarvabhaiṣajyarasān svāhā niryātaya cittaprītiḥ aiḥ saḥ maṃ tṛptiṃ kuru*.
*Ṇa ma li*—to these honored ones who partake of the food:
*Maṃ ya ni ve ni ḍu*, I most sincerely offer: *Phaṭ kṛtyāyāḥ pratisarāyai kṣiye prasarasi*.
Oṃ ahara ahara sarvaviniyadara pūrti svāhā. Recite this seven times; it is used for all three families. As for the mudrā: turn both palms upward.
The sides of the two ring fingers touch each other; the tips of the two index fingers are slightly bent and pressed against the sides of the middle fingers;
the two thumbs are pressed against the sides of the two index fingers.
This mudrā resembles the gesture of cupping water and is used for making offerings across all three families.
Furthermore, the mantra for offering food to the Buddha Family is:
"Oṃ che na mi ni svāhā. Recite this seven times. The mantra for offering food to the Lotus Family is:
"Oṃ vi lu kiṃ ni svāhā. Recite this seven times. The mantra for offering food to the Vajra Family is:

"Oṃ vajrīṇi vajrajvālāye svāhā. Recite this seven times. Next, as previously described for removing impurities up to [attaining] a lustrous appearance, light the lamps while reciting this mantra and the root mantra, and further offer them while performing the hand gestures (*mudrā*).
The mantra for offering to Dīpaṃkara is:
"Ra-kṣa-ṇam-svāhā. This purifies the body and is able to remove ignorance;
these [offerings] are reverently presented with *pūjā*. *Vidhāra*. Two.

Recite seven times: *He-he* (haya), *nan* (na), *oṃ*, *a-lu-ka-ya*, *a-la-ka-ya*, *sarva-vinayadara-pūrti-te svāhā*. Three.
Regarding the mudrā for use in all three families: form a fist with the right hand, extend the middle finger, and press the tip of the thumb against it while holding it upright.
This is the *Dīpaṅkara-sevana-mudrā*, used throughout the three families.
Furthermore, the mantra for offering lamps to the Buddha Family is:
“Oṃ ara-ma-ra-khaṃ-ṭi-te-ri-ṇi svāhā. Recite this three times. The mantra for offering lamps to the Lotus Family is:
“Oṃ jvālani ṇi rucana-kari hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this seven times. The mantra for offering lamps to the Vajra Family is:

"Oṃ vimalatāluñcaraṇa hūṃ phaṭ. (Recite seven times. Next, regarding the mental offering performed with mantras and mudrās: even if one is unable to provide offerings such as scented unguents up to lamps, merely reciting the aforementioned mantras for the offering of scented unguents and so forth, while performing the corresponding mudrās, also constitutes a complete and perfect offering.

Next, regarding the offering made by means of mental visualization: one mentally conjures waters and land flowers that are not claimed by any owner, filling the entirety of space throughout the ten directions;
as well as clouds of exquisite human and celestial unguents, burning incense, lamps, banners and streamers, precious parasols, various drums and music, and songs and dances.
Chanting, pearl nets, hanging jeweled bells, flower garlands, white whisks, exquisite chimes and gongs, *kiṅkiṇī* nets,
wish-fulfilling jewel trees, clouds of celestial garments, various heavenly foods and delicacies of supreme fragrance and flavor,
palaces and towers adorned with precious pillars, and all manner of celestial ornaments for the body.
With clouds of crowns, necklaces, and so forth—such as these, the practitioner directs the mind to pervade the entirety of space;
making offerings with such a sincere heart is the most supreme and excellent.

Therefore, the practitioner should practice this dharma with a resolute mind; by directing the mind toward making offerings, reciting mantras, and performing mudrās, all that has been visualized above will be fully accomplished.

The mantra is: Oṃ sarvathā kaṃ guhna-ade sa-phara-hi-ma-ga-ga-na-khaṃ svāhā. Recite this seven times. As for the mudrā: interlace the two hands in *añjali* (palms joined), with the right hand pressing over the left, and place it upon the crown of the head. This is the mudrā of the "Accomplishment of the Mind-Offering Vessel."

In performing any offering, one should possess this method: with utmost sincerity and faith, the presentation of argha water—all accomplished through the recitation of mantras and the application of mudrās—and by directing the mind while joining the palms and placing them upon the crown of the head, the rite of complete and perfect offering is then fulfilled.

Next, regarding the praise of the Dharma: first, one should give rise to faith with utmost sincerity and reverence, praising the virtues of the Buddha; next, those of the Dharma and the Sangha; and finally, those of Avalokiteśvara, Vajrapāṇi, and other Bodhisattvas.
Praising the Buddha’s virtues:
“The World-Honored One of Great Compassion, The Guide endowed with all arts,
An ocean of boundless merit— I now pay homage with my head at his feet.”
Next, the praise of the virtues of the Dharma:
"The Dharma of purity free from desire, Which can eliminate all evil realms;
The true tranquility, the ultimate truth— I prostrate to that which abides in accordance with it."
Next, the praise of the Sangha’s virtues:
“Having well attained the path of liberation, Abiding wondrously in all the stages of awakening,
Peerless field of merit— To this I now take refuge.”
Next, he praised Avalokiteśvara:
"O Great Auspiciousness of all Buddhas, Perfectly endowed with venerable virtues,
Named Avalokiteśvara, I take refuge in you who are eternally tranquil and silent."
Next, he praised Vajrapāṇi:
“Greatly powerful and wondrously wrathful, Accomplisher of the Great Vidyārāja,
Tamer of those difficult to subdue— I take refuge in Vajrapāṇi.”

Regarding the great bodhisattvas whom one has previously taken refuge in, one should praise them as one wishes, according to the sūtras; likewise, when one desires to praise other tutelary deities, they too should be praised.

Next, one should repent of all transgressions; next, rejoice in all merits; next, one should issue invitations, further entreating that [the Buddhas] remain in the world to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
Next, take refuge in the Triple Gem; next, generate the bodhicitta; next, one should make aspirations.
First, regarding the confession of transgressions:

“I only pray that all Buddhas of the ten directions, all great Bodhisattvas, and the noble Saṅgha of Arhats will keep me in mind and bear witness to me: whether in this life or in my previous lives, since beginningless birth and death, I have been distressed in body and mind by all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion, and have extensively committed various sins. Toward the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; toward my parents, teachers, and elders; toward all Bodhisattvas, all holy ones, and other sentient beings—whether virtuous or lacking virtue—I have acted with unrestrained threefold karma, committing various offenses. Whether acting myself, inciting others, or rejoicing upon seeing others act, such sins are immeasurable and boundless. Before all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, I now reveal them with a sincere heart and repent with deep earnestness.”
After having performed this single repentance, I shall never again commit such deeds.
I only pray that all Buddhas of the ten directions and all great Bodhisattvas will compassionately bear witness to this, so that my karmic obstructions may be extinguished.

Regarding "taking refuge in the Triple Gem": for the sake of eliminating the various sufferings of sentient beings, one should take refuge in the Triple Gem in this manner, reflecting upon the individual merits and virtues of each member of the Triple Gem, and prostrating with the head touching the ground. Taking refuge in this way, one should speak these words:

"I, [Name], from this present body until I sit at the site of enlightenment, take refuge in the unsurpassed three bodies of the Tathāgata, take refuge in the Dharma-treasury of the Vaipulya Mahāyāna, and take refuge in the assembly of all non-regressive Bodhisattvas. I pray that all Buddhas of the ten directions and all great Bodhisattvas will compassionately accept me."
"One should take refuge in the Three Jewels in this manner.

For one who has resolved upon bodhicitta, this bodhicitta is called the unsurpassed seed of the Mahāyāna; because it can bestow upon sentient beings the wondrous fruit of ambrosial liberation, if one practices with earnest diligence, it can produce siddhi."

“Desiring to sever the immeasurable sufferings within the realm of sentient beings, to free them from the defilements of afflictions and transcend the three evil paths, and to eliminate the immeasurable sufferings of taking birth within the three realms of existence, I shall now act as their place of refuge. For those who are without a master or reliance, I am their support; for those crossing the ocean of birth and death, I am their captain; for those who have lost their way, I am the good path; for those without protection, I am their savior. I shall remove suffering and bestow happiness. All the afflictions and secondary afflictions of all sentient beings, I shall eliminate for them. They shall constantly contemplate wholesome karma and not dwell on unwholesome conditions. Adorning their bodies with various merits and wisdom, they shall diligently and uninterruptedly cultivate the six *pāramitās*, benefiting sentient beings and practicing this merit together.”

Whatever merit and wisdom I have cultivated in this life or in other lives for the benefit of sentient beings, may all afflictions and secondary afflictions be subdued; may I diligently cultivate wholesome qualities until reaching enlightenment, and may my mind be free from attachment to any unwholesome conditions.
"One should thus resolve upon bodhicitta.

Furthermore, one should cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; dwell in stillness within a single object of focus; constantly contemplate the six recollections; observe the mind so as to accord with the principle of nirvana; and forget all conceptual attachments, relinquishing and forever eliminating them."

Regarding the subsequent practice of making superior vows while seated upon one's seat: just as the Bodhisattvas cultivate wholesome qualities and extensively make superior vows for the benefit of sentient beings, so too shall all my own roots of goodness be.
Furthermore, I vow that all sentient beings may be able to eliminate the sufferings of the hells and other realms, fulfill their merit and virtue, and realize the bliss of nirvāṇa.

Moreover, I vow that all sentient beings shall abound in wealth and treasures, always practice courageous giving, be fully endowed with wisdom, constantly maintain great patience, delight in creating virtuous conditions, attain the knowledge of past lives, and compassionately regard all sentient beings; may all sentient beings, wherever they are born, always obtain these various kinds of supreme matters.

Regarding the mudrā for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*): as for this mudrā, one interlaces the two earth-fingers (*pṛthivī-aṅguli*) of both hands within the palms; one presses the two water-fingers (*ap-aṅguli*) against each other above them; one extends the two fire-fingers (*tejas-aṅguli*) straight upward with their tips touching; one bends the two wind-fingers (*vāyu-aṅguli*) behind the fire-fingers so that they do not touch; and one extends the two space-fingers (*ākāśa-aṅguli*) straight upward, positioned beneath the second joints of the two fire-fingers. Thus the mudrā is formed.
This is the Mudrā of the Body of Cundī.
Stir the water with this mudrā while reciting the mantra seven times, or twenty-one times, or one hundred and eight times, and bathe as you wish.

Furthermore, the characteristics of the separate seal are described: one visualizes the space wheel (*ākāśa-cakra*) as the wings, holds the earth wheel (*pṛthivī-cakra*) as the fingernails, and stands the remaining three wheels upright, forming the shape of a three-pronged *vajra*. This may also be employed according to the previous method; this is the *karma-mudrā* of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī-ghoṣa (Muṇḍarī).

After consecrating the earth, apply the two mudrās and mantras. Regarding these mudrās, the text states: "Form the inner fist (*muṣṭi*), join the two thumbs with their tips meeting to form the shape of a vajra, and use it to pierce the earth three times; this is the method."

Furthermore, with the hands in the inner-bound mudrā (*antarabandha*), extend and join the two thumbs (*aṅguṣṭha*); place the two index fingers (*tarjanī*) within the joined index fingers; likewise, extend and join the two ring fingers (*anāmikā*). Then, apply this mudrā to the earth, turning it three times to the right, whereby the protection is established.
Next, proceeding up to the mudrā for expelling obstacles, one should perform the recitation according to the Dharma at each respective time.
Furthermore, there are four essential methods for adding to the recitation:
namely, recitation by counting syllables, recitation by counting times, recitation by signs, and augmented recitation.

Having completed the recitation, one should earnestly seek the fulfillment of whatever vows one harbors and whatever accomplishments one intends to achieve; thereafter, one should perform recitation and *homā* (fire sacrifice), for by acting according to the ritual law, the wishes harbored in one's heart will be swiftly fulfilled and accomplished as desired.
Even if the root manual does not explicitly mention homa, one should perform it according to the ritual rules for the sake of attaining siddhi.
There are two kinds of objects for accomplishment:
first, substances such as orpiment and vermilion; second, the purity of mind.

According to the medicinal substances, receive them in accordance with the ritual, select and purify them, and pray for auspicious conditions; then, each one shall be consecrated according to its respective root rite in accordance with the Dharma.

The preparation for the consecration sprinkling (*abhiṣeka*) requires three conditions: namely, the mantra, medicinal substances, and one’s own body. Only when these three conditions are complete should one seek *siddhi*.

First, one contemplates each individual characteristic of both the internal and external, and, possessing diligent practice, acts in accordance with the precepts of the mantra. In order to eliminate immeasurable unwholesome karma, one extensively cultivates pure and white dharmas according to the instructions so that sins may be eradicated; then, by reciting the mantra, one eventually attains the accomplishment of *siddhi*.

Furthermore, cause the pure and white karma to increase and bring it to ultimate perfection; then, one should recite the mantra according to the ritual method until the attainment of siddhi is achieved.

Just as one who contemplates the mind relies upon abiding in a single object, binding the mindfulness and focusing the thought on the tip of the nose so that there is no distraction and it accords with samādhi;
so too should the practitioner of recitation act: by binding the mind through focused thought and projecting it into the mantra, one shall attain accomplishment by means of this focal point.

To perform the rite of accomplishment (*sādhana*), one should prepare the necessary seats and mantras. On the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day of the waxing moon; on days when the moon or sun undergoes an eclipse; on days of great earthquakes; or from the first to the fifteenth day of the new year—on such days as these, one should perform the rites of accomplishment.

However, according to this fundamental method, everything must be fully prepared. Having already selected an excellent site for recitation, one should perform the rite of protective binding (*rakṣā*) at that location. One should construct a maṇḍala according to the specific *siddhi* method, and following the rules for the maṇḍala of the particular mantra being held as well as other related methods, one should install the deities of the ten directions. Having made offerings according to the ritual and prepared all the requisites, including assistants, one should bind and protect oneself and others before entering the practice of recitation and performing the rites for accomplishment (*sādhanā*).
Upon reaching the point of beginning the construction, he offered this short praise to Vajra-Heruka:
"I take refuge in the Vajra-Headed One, The subduer of all māras,
Who possesses the manifold practices of Samantabhadra, And is an ocean of boundless merit."
Abiding in this originally existent body, eternally quiescent without beginning or end,
you manifest wondrous functions to grant all vows, subduing Māra and extinguishing the three poisons.
Having transformed former practices, you bring ultimate salvation to all sentient beings.
